problem_plain: Building and running AI systems at the scale of real products means solving a grab-bag of practical problems that do not fit neatly into any one box: training models spread across dozens of machines without drowning in the time it takes those machines to share results, stopping the software that runs those models from swelling to a size that eats up memory, cutting the amount of bookkeeping data that training needs to hold in memory at once, making sure that performance measurements reported in research papers actually mean what they claim to mean, counting the carbon emitted not just by running chips but by building them in the first place, and squeezing large datasets so they travel and store faster. None of these is glamorous, but all of them quietly set a ceiling on how fast or how cheaply AI can actually move forward.
why_plain: AI workloads bump up against two scarce resources that money cannot infinitely multiply: memory space and how fast data moves (bandwidth). Every source of waste — software libraries stuffed with code nobody uses, redundant bookkeeping data sitting in memory during training, slow result-sharing across machines on different continents, or raw data sent uncompressed — burns real time and real energy at scale.
approach_plain: The papers here attack this kind of hidden waste from many angles at once: stripping away software that is compiled but never actually called, replacing expensive per-weight training bookkeeping with a compact mathematical stand-in that reaches the same answer, redesigning how machines share training results so they do it far less often across slow long-distance links, squeezing numbers down at the hardware level so less data needs to travel, and replacing misleading summary statistics in research papers with ones that are mathematically sound. The common thread is finding and eliminating hidden waste — in software, in memory, in network round-trips, in how results are reported.

groups.heading: Shrinking memory used during model training
groups.explain: Training a large AI model requires storing not just the model's weights (its learned numbers) but also the training optimizer's running bookkeeping — figures that track how each weight has been shifting over time, used to give each weight its own personal step size. For a model with 7 billion weights, that bookkeeping alone fills 28 gigabytes of memory, crowding out space for data and forcing the use of more machines. The paper here finds a clever way to store far less bookkeeping without changing what the training process actually learns.

papers.name: APOLLO
papers.gloss: Stores training bookkeeping as a compact mathematical sketch instead of full tables, slashing optimizer memory from 28 GB to 1.6 GB for a 7-billion-weight model with no loss in training quality, and enabling 3x higher throughput by fitting bigger batches on the same hardware.

groups.heading: Training across slow or unreliable network links
groups.explain: Standard distributed training requires every machine to share its weight updates with every other machine after each and every training step. Inside one data center on fast private cables that is fine, but it becomes a stranglehold when machines sit in different cities or are connected only by ordinary internet. The papers here redesign the sharing pattern so that machines do many local steps before talking to each other, dramatically cutting how much data must cross the slow link.

papers.name: Photon
papers.gloss: Lets clusters in different cities each train on their own for many steps before sharing results, cutting the data that must cross slow long-distance links 500-fold for a 7-billion-weight model and reducing total training time 35% versus a centralized approach, while actually improving model quality.

papers.name: JaxPP
papers.gloss: Adds to an existing AI research toolkit the ability to split a model's layers across many machines like an assembly line, so each machine handles one stage and passes its output to the next, enabling efficient training across slower links between machines.

groups.heading: Removing dead weight from machine-learning software
groups.explain: The software libraries that power GPU-based machine learning ship with huge amounts of pre-compiled instructions — code covering dozens of different GPU chip generations and every possible operation type — but any one training run uses only a tiny slice of it. All that unused code still occupies memory, slows program startup, and crowds out the scarce space the GPU needs for actual work. The paper here builds a tool to find what is actually called and remove the rest permanently.

papers.name: Negativa-ML
papers.gloss: Watches which pieces of GPU software any given workload actually loads and calls at runtime, then permanently strips out everything else from the library files, shrinking GPU code by up to 75% and cutting peak GPU memory use by up to 70%.

groups.heading: Compressing scientific and AI data at wire speed
groups.explain: Scientific simulations and large AI datasets produce enormous volumes of decimal numbers — the kind computers use for real-world measurements — faster than storage and network links can handle them. Compressing those numbers before storing or sending them buys back that speed, but existing tools force a choice between going fast and compressing well. The paper here closes that gap, targeting the specific internal bit patterns that floating-point decimal numbers use, on both regular processors and GPUs.

papers.gloss: Four new lossless compression methods that exploit the internal bit layout of decimal numbers to squeeze data without any information loss, reaching over 500 GB per second on a modern GPU while also beating most existing tools on how tightly they compress.

groups.heading: Accounting for the carbon cost of building and running hardware
groups.explain: A chip's environmental footprint comes from two very different places: the electricity it consumes while running (its operating carbon), and the enormous industrial process that manufactured it (its built-in carbon — the pollution created before it ever turned on). These two costs trade off against each other in non-obvious ways. A chip packed with more circuitry is faster but took more energy to make; running fewer, larger chips for longer saves manufacturing carbon but may burn more electricity over time. The paper here builds a framework to optimize both costs at once rather than treating them separately.

papers.name: CORDOBA
papers.gloss: Creates a single combined score — total carbon multiplied by how long the job takes — that weighs both manufacturing and running costs together, uses it to eliminate 98% of chip design options automatically, and finds that placing memory directly on top of the processor (stacking chips together) improves this combined score by 6.9 times.

groups.heading: Making performance measurements honest and comparable
groups.explain: Researchers report how much faster their new design is by averaging speed-up ratios across many tests. But the standard way of averaging those ratios — the geometric mean taught in statistics class — gives the wrong answer for speed-up comparisons: it can declare one chip the winner even when the other chip is faster on every single individual test. Separately, specialized chips for tasks like tracking where a VR headset user is looking need their own purpose-built measures. The papers here tackle measurement correctness at the level of method.

papers.gloss: Proves with algebra that the standard way of averaging speed-up numbers across benchmarks gives wrong answers, identifies the correct replacement (a different kind of average called the harmonic mean), and shows the two methods can declare opposite chips the winner.

papers.name: POLO / POLONet
papers.gloss: Builds an AI model and a matching custom chip that together render VR images at full quality only in the small spot where the user's eyes are actually pointed, cutting the end-to-end delay 3.9 times compared to previous eye-tracking approaches.

Speeds up GPU-based text pattern matching — used in database searches and log analysis — by 19.5 times, by loading each block of input text just once and checking all patterns against it together, instead of reloading the same text once per pattern.

connect: Every paper here ultimately fights the same root constraint: the gap between how fast a processor can crunch numbers and how fast data can actually reach it. Whether the fix is squeezing data before it travels, replacing bulky training bookkeeping with a compact stand-in, sharing training results far less often across slow long-distance links, or stripping unused code that crowds out working data — each solution reclaims bandwidth or memory capacity that raw computing power alone cannot create.
